--- jupyter: stats --- # Logistic Regression Logistic regression is a classification method for binary outcomes. It models the conditional probability of the positive class as a function of the predictors. For a binary response, write $$ Y\in\{0,1\}. $$ The main target is the conditional probability $$ p(x)=\Pr(Y=1\mid X=x). $$ Once this probability is estimated, it can be used for several related tasks: - probability estimation; - ranking observations by risk; - hard classification after choosing a threshold. ::: {.callout-note} ## Model and decision Logistic regression estimates probabilities. A classification threshold then converts those probabilities into decisions. These are related, but they are not the same problem. ::: ## Modeling Binary Outcomes In linear regression, we model a quantitative response by $$ Y=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\cdots+\beta_px_p+\varepsilon. $$ This is not appropriate for a binary response if the fitted value is interpreted as a probability. A linear function can be below 0 or above 1. Logistic regression solves this problem by modeling the probability through the logistic function. Let $$ \eta(x) = \beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\cdots+\beta_px_p = x^\top\beta, $$ where $x^\top\beta$ includes the intercept term if the first component of $x$ is 1. Logistic regression defines $$ p(x) = \Pr(Y=1\mid X=x) = \frac{\exp(\eta(x))}{1+\exp(\eta(x))} = \frac{1}{1+\exp(-\eta(x))}. $$ This guarantees $$ 0c,\\ 0, & \hat p(x)\le c. \end{cases} $$ The default threshold is often $c=0.5$, but this is not always the best choice. Changing the threshold changes the confusion matrix and therefore changes accuracy, precision, recall, false positive rate, and F1 score. Suppose a false positive has cost $C_{FP}$ and a false negative has cost $C_{FN}$. If $\hat p(x)$ is a calibrated estimate of $p(x)$, then the expected cost of predicting positive is $$ \text{Cost}(1\mid x) = C_{FP}\{1-p(x)\}, $$ and the expected cost of predicting negative is $$ \text{Cost}(0\mid x) = C_{FN}p(x). $$ Predict positive when $$ C_{FP}\{1-p(x)\} < C_{FN}p(x). $$ Solving gives the decision-theoretic threshold $$ c^* = \frac{C_{FP}}{C_{FP}+C_{FN}}. $$ If false negatives are more costly, then $C_{FN}$ is large and the threshold becomes smaller. The classifier predicts the positive class more aggressively. ::: {.callout-note} ## Threshold tuning Threshold tuning changes the decision rule built on top of $\hat p(x)$. It does not refit the logistic regression model or change the fitted probabilities. ::: ## Logistic Regression in `sklearn` `sklearn` is usually the better choice for predictive workflows, train-test splits, pipelines, cross-validation, and threshold tuning.
